strengths: Identifies and formalizes a practically important and underexplored problem setting combining three real-world challenges simultaneously: channel-wise asynchronous sampling periods, block-wise test-time missingness, and inter-channel dependency, motivated with concrete industrial examples.

Provides a clear theoretical/analytical explanation (Appendix B) of why linear interpolation introduces spectral distortion (amplitude attenuation, spectral leakage, phase delay), which nicely supports the design choice of avoiding interpolation.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three modified public benchmarks and one real-world industrial (LNG carrier) dataset, with multiple architecturally diverse baselines (Transformer, CNN, GNN, MLP-based).

Thorough ablation studies: component-wise ablation (dependency/asynchrony/missingness), six variants of attention masking strategy, number of channel tokens, robustness to varying test-time input lengths, and frequency-domain fidelity analysis.
Also validates the model in the conventional (fully-observed, synchronously sampled) forecasting setting, showing it remains competitive there, which strengthens the generality claim.
Reports error bars over multiple seeds for main results, improving credibility of comparisons.
weaknesses: The 'asynchronous' benchmark datasets are synthetically constructed by downsampling originally synchronous data (ETTm1, Weather, Monash), so it's unclear whether this fully captures the complexities of genuinely asynchronous real-world sensor networks; results on the single real industrial dataset (CHS) are less extensively analyzed and not clearly available for reproducibility.

Performance improvements over strong baselines (e.g., TimeXer, PatchTST) are often modest (roughly 3-10%), and given the reported error bars, some gains may be only marginally significant in certain settings/datasets.

Despite extensively discussing the irregular/asynchronous time series literature in Related Work, the paper does not empirically compare against any of these dedicated irregular-sampling methods (e.g., ContiFormer, Raindrop, GraFITi-style models), which would be a natural and more direct baseline category for the asynchronous setting, rather than only comparing to standard synchronous forecasters fed interpolated data.

The core architectural novelty is somewhat incremental, combining known ideas (global/CLS-like summary tokens, patch dropout/masking, frequency-informed patch length selection, read-only attention masking) into a new configuration rather than introducing fundamentally new mechanisms.

The authors acknowledge a genuine scalability limitation (quadratic attention cost growing with channel count) but provide no empirical runtime/memory/parameter-count comparison against baselines to quantify this trade-off.
No mention of code or the real-world CHS dataset release, limiting reproducibility, particularly since baseline reimplementations (e.g., CrossGNN) and custom dataset constructions are involved.
The number of channel tokens and masking strategy appear to require per-dataset tuning (Table 4, Table 10), suggesting sensitivity to hyperparameters that may complicate deployment in new settings.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and underexplored combination of three practical challenges simultaneously (channel dependency, asynchronous sampling, and missingness), rather than treating them in isolation as most prior work does.

Extensive empirical evaluation across six datasets (four adapted benchmarks, one industrial LNG dataset, one air-quality dataset), covering two case studies (asynchrony-only and asynchrony+missingness), with consistent improvements over a wide range of baselines spanning Transformer, CNN/MLP/GNN, and irregular-time-series architectures.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of channel dependence, dynamic patching, and patch masking, plus additional ablations on channel embeddings, patch length choices, and six attention-masking variants.

Good supporting analyses beyond raw accuracy numbers: frequency-domain analysis quantifying interpolation-induced spectral distortion (theoretically and empirically), scalability analysis (channel count and input length), and robustness to input-length variability at test time.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, dataset construction procedures, error bars over multiple seeds, and an explicit reproducibility/ethics statement.
weaknesses: Core architectural ingredients (channel-level summary tokens, frequency-guided variable-length patching, random patch/token dropout as a masking strategy, read-only attention masks) are each drawn fairly directly from existing works (iTransformer/TimeXer, Moirai/LightGTS, PatchDropout, read-only prompt attention); the paper's contribution is primarily their combination and adaptation, which is somewhat incremental rather than conceptually novel.

Reported performance gains over the strongest baseline (TimeXer) are often small in absolute terms (frequently 0.01-0.03 CMSE/CMAE), raising questions about the practical significance of the improvement relative to the added architectural complexity (extra channel tokens, custom attention masks, frequency-based patch length search).

Most 'practical' asynchronous datasets (ETT1/ETT2, Weather, SolarWind) are synthetically constructed by resampling standard benchmarks with manually assigned per-channel sampling periods, rather than being genuinely irregular real-world data; only EPA and the private CHS dataset reflect truly heterogeneous real sampling, somewhat weakening the 'real-world' framing.

The optimal number of channel tokens (1-3) is dataset-dependent and must be tuned per dataset (Table 4), reducing the plug-and-play nature of the method and adding another hyperparameter to search compared to simpler baselines.

Several irregular-time-series baselines (ContiFormer, t-PatchGNN, Hi-Patch, CrossGNN, BiTGraph) were reimplemented/integrated into a different (TimesNet-based) codebase than their original release, which could introduce implementation discrepancies that affect the fairness of comparison, and ContiFormer's ODE solver was approximated for efficiency, potentially altering its true behavior.

Scalability analysis shows OOM at 280 channels on a 24GB GPU and quadratic growth in runtime/memory with channel count, which could limit applicability to larger real-world sensor networks (e.g., industrial systems with hundreds of channels), a point the paper acknowledges as future work.

strengths: Tackles a genuinely underexplored combination of practical challenges (channel-wise asynchronous sampling, block-wise test-time missingness, and cross-channel dependency) that most prior forecasting work addresses only in isolation.

Extensive experimental coverage across multiple modified public benchmarks and one private industrial dataset, plus a wide range of baseline categories (CD/CI Transformers, CNN/GNN/MLP, irregular-sampling and missingness-aware models).

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (component removal, masking-strategy variants, channel-token count, input-length robustness) and a scalability analysis showing where the architecture breaks down (OOM at ~280 channels).
The frequency-domain analysis of interpolation-induced distortion (amplitude attenuation, spectral leakage, phase delay) is a nice theoretical framing that motivates the interpolation-free design.
Error bars over multiple seeds are reported in the appendix, which is good practice for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core architectural novelty is limited: the paper explicitly acknowledges its channel-token idea 'resembles' iTransformer/TimeXer summary tokens, and the frequency-guided dynamic patching and PatchDropout-based masking are directly repurposed from prior univariate/vision works rather than newly developed for this setting; the contribution reads largely as an engineering integration of existing components under a unifying mask.

Reported gains over the strongest baselines are frequently marginal (e.g., ETT2: 0.377 vs 0.380 CMSE; ETT1: 0.399 vs 0.411; CHS CMAE ties with tPatchGNN) and often fall within one standard deviation shown in the appendix tables, raising doubts about the practical significance of the improvements.

The 'practical' asynchronous benchmarks are all synthetically constructed by resampling standard datasets (ETTm1/2, Weather, Monash Solar/Wind) according to the authors' own heuristics, rather than being genuinely irregular real-world data; this raises concern that the benchmark setup was designed to favor the proposed model rather than reflecting an externally validated notion of real-world asynchrony.

The evaluation protocol embeds an architectural advantage into the problem setup itself: regular baselines are forced through lossy linear interpolation while CTF operates interpolation-free by design, so part of the reported gap reflects the preprocessing choice rather than a controlled comparison of model capacity; even the 'interpolation-free' modified TimeXer variant only partially closes this gap, suggesting the benefit is more from problem framing than from the proposed attention mechanism.

Several irregular/missingness baselines (ContiFormer, Hi-Patch, t-PatchGNN, BiTGraph, CrossGNN) were reimplemented into the TimesNet framework rather than run with their original codebases, which could introduce implementation discrepancies that are hard to verify and may understate their true performance.

The optimal number of channel tokens (1, 2, or 3) must be tuned per dataset without a principled selection rule; the post-hoc explanation based on 'channel similarity and diversity' is speculative and not independently validated.

Ablation results show some components contribute very little in certain regimes (e.g., 'w/o patch masking' only changes CMSE from 0.452 to 0.458 at m=0.375), weakening the claim that all three components are strictly necessary in a strong, consistent sense.
The private CHS dataset limits reproducibility, and code availability is only promised 'upon publication' rather than provided for review.

Standard MSE-based loss and CMSE metric are used throughout despite the paper's own discussion (Section G) acknowledging that MSE fails to penalize amplitude attenuation/over-smoothing, meaning the paper's own evaluation may not fully capture the qualitative advantages it claims (e.g., spectral fidelity) in the main quantitative tables.

Scalability analysis reveals real limits (OOM at 280 channels, quadratic attention cost) that could constrain applicability to larger real-world industrial systems, which somewhat undercuts the 'real-world' framing emphasized in the title.
